report.title: Leaked IAM access key abuse: from repository leak to crypto-mining and S3 theft
report.summary: A CI service IAM access key committed to a public GitHub repo was validated within 11 minutes. The actor enumerated the account, created a backdoor user with admin rights, disabled CloudTrail logging, launched GPU instances for cryptomining in two regions, and bulk-downloaded S3 objects from a customer-data bucket. All subsequent activity pivoted on the new backuser account or reactivated disabled keys in a second account.
threat_actors: automated actor (validated key from Tor exit node)
targets: CI service accounts, AWS accounts with S3 buckets, GPU compute resources

behaviors.description: Actor validated leaked AWS credentials by calling STS GetCallerIdentity and enumerating account resources (IAM users, attached policies, S3 buckets, EC2 instances across all regions) from a Tor exit node.

observables.note: User agent from Tor exit node
First API call validating the key
Enumeration of EC2 instances across all regions

behaviors.evidence: The first calls came from a Tor exit node (185.220.101.34) with the user agent `aws-cli/1.33.12 Python/3.11.2 Linux/6.1.0-kali` and were made by the leaked identity `arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/ci-deployer`: sts:GetCallerIdentity, iam:ListUsers, iam:ListAttachedUserPolicies, iam:GetAccountAuthorizationDetails, s3:ListBuckets, ec2:DescribeInstances (every region).

behaviors.description: Actor created a new IAM user 'backup-svc' and attached the full AdministratorAccess policy to establish persistence via a backdoor account.
behaviors.evidence: The actor created a new user and gave it full administrative rights: iam:CreateUser userName=backup-svc, iam:CreateAccessKey userName=backup-svc, iam:AttachUserPolicy userName=backup-svc policyArn=arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess, iam:CreateLoginProfile userName=backup-svc (console password set).

behaviors.description: Actor disabled CloudTrail organization trail and deleted the trail, and deleted the GuardDuty detector in us-east-1 to evade detection.
behaviors.evidence: In `us-east-1` the actor stopped and later deleted the organisation trail: cloudtrail:StopLogging name=org-trail, cloudtrail:DeleteTrail name=org-trail. It also called guardduty:DeleteDetector in the same region.

behaviors.description: Actor launched GPU-accelerated EC2 compute instances (p4d.24xlarge) in two unused regions using the backdoor account, each with user data that installed XMRig cryptominer.
behaviors.evidence: Within an hour the actor launched sixteen `p4d.24xlarge` instances in `ap-south-1` and `sa-east-1`, regions the organisation had never used, each with user data that installed XMRig: ec2:RunInstances instanceType=p4d.24xlarge count=8 (ap-south-1), ec2:RunInstances instanceType=p4d.24xlarge count=8 (sa-east-1).

behaviors.description: Actor listed and downloaded objects from the bucket acme-customer-exports using S3 ListObjectsV2 followed by thousands of GetObject calls, exfiltrating ~23 GB over 40 minutes from a Tor exit node.

observables.note: thousands of calls over 40 minutes, 23 GB total

behaviors.evidence: The actor listed and downloaded objects from the bucket `acme-customer-exports` using `s3:ListObjectsV2` followed by thousands of `s3:GetObject` calls over 40 minutes, 23 GB in total, all from the Tor exit node.

behaviors.description: Actor attempted to grant public read access to the S3 bucket by calling PutBucketPolicy with Principal "*", which was blocked by the organization's SCP.

observables.note: Principal: "*" read access on bucket acme-customer-exports

behaviors.evidence: The actor also called `s3:PutBucketPolicy` on the bucket to grant `Principal: "*"` read access, which was caught by the organisation's SCP and returned `AccessDenied`.

behaviors.description: Actor reactivated a disabled IAM access key of an existing user in a second victim account and attached AdministratorAccess policy via role assumption.

observables.note: reactivate a disabled key of an existing user
add AdministratorAccess to a role it could assume

behaviors.evidence: In a second victim account the actor instead called `iam:UpdateAccessKey` to reactivate a disabled key of an existing user and `iam:AttachRolePolicy` to add `AdministratorAccess` to a role it could assume.

behaviors.description: Actor used a Tor exit node IP (185.220.101.34) with distinctive AWS CLI user agent to perform all malicious actions, masking origin.
behaviors.evidence: The first calls came from a Tor exit node (185.220.101.34) with the user agent `aws-cli/1.33.12 Python/3.11.2 Linux/6.1.0-kali`.

candidates.title: Mass S3 Data Exfiltration via GetObject from Tor Exit Node
candidates.rationale: Actor exfiltrated 23 GB over 40 minutes via thousands of s3:GetObject calls on bucket 'acme-customer-exports' from Tor exit node 185.220.101.34. Extreme volume + Tor exit node + known customer data bucket = very high signal.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate bulk downloads from same bucket by legitimate ETL jobs; mitigate by scoring on source IP reputation (Tor exit), volume (>1 GB / 10 min), and unusual user-agent.

candidates.title: S3 Bucket Policy Modification to Public Access (Principal "*")
candidates.rationale: Actor called s3:PutBucketPolicy with Principal "*" on bucket acme-customer-exports; blocked by SCP but intent is clear—public read grant on customer data bucket. Policy change to Principal "*" on sensitive bucket is extremely high signal regardless of SCP block.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate policy updates by admins; mitigate by alerting only when Principal contains "*" or overly broad conditions on sensitive buckets, and alert even on AccessDenied.

candidates.title: IAM Access Key Reactivation + AdministratorAccess Attachment via Role Assumption
candidates.rationale: Actor reactivated a disabled IAM access key (iam:UpdateAccessKey) and attached AdministratorAccess to an assumable role (iam:AttachRolePolicy) in a second victim account. Credential reactivation + immediate privilege escalation via role assumption is a high-signal persistence + privilege-escalation chain.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate key rotation or role policy updates by admins; mitigate by alerting on reactivation of previously disabled keys combined with attachment of AWS managed AdministratorAccess policy to assumable roles within short time window.

candidates.title: Distinctive AWS CLI User-Agent from Tor Exit Nodes
candidates.rationale: All observed malicious API calls originated from Tor exit nodes (185.220.101.34, 185.220.101.34) with a distinctive, version-pinned AWS CLI user-agent string 'aws-cli/1.33.12 Python/3.11.2 Linux/6.11.2' (duplicated substring). This UA + Tor IP combination is a high-fidelity actor fingerprint across all observed activity.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate users behind Tor or using same CLI version; mitigate by requiring Tor exit node IP reputation match + exact UA string match + API calls on sensitive resources (S3 data buckets, IAM, S3 policy).

candidates.title: S3 Mass Enumeration (ListObjectsV2) of Customer Export Bucket as Pre-Exfiltration Recon
candidates.rationale: Actor performed s3:ListObjectsV2 on bucket 'acme-customer-exports' followed by 40 minutes of GetObject calls. The ListObjectsV2 enumeration of a sensitive customer-data bucket from a Tor exit node is the reconnaissance phase; detecting it early can trigger before mass download.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate inventory jobs listing the same bucket; mitigate by scoring on source IP reputation (Tor), unusual user-agent, and absence of known inventory role ARNs.

rules.title: AWS S3 Bucket Policy Set to Public Read via Principal "*"
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: 'AWS S3 Bucket Policy Set to Public Read via Principal "*"'
id: 47b09531-b141-47c6-ad91-12c243091843
status: experimental
description: 'Detects attempts to modify an S3 bucket policy to grant public read access using Principal "*", indicative of
  impact-oriented credential abuse even when blocked by SCPs.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.impact
- attack.t1529
logsource:
  category: cloud_api
  product: aws
  service: cloudtrail
detection:
  selection:
    eventSource: s3.amazonaws.com
    eventName: PutBucketPolicy
    'requestParameters.policy|contains|all':
    - '"Principal"'
    - '"*"'
    - '"s3:GetObject"'
  filter_specific_account:
    'requestParameters.policy|contains': '"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::'
  filter_static_website:
    'requestParameters.policy|contains|all':
    - '"Principal":"*"'
    - '"Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::'
    - '"Effect":"Allow"'
  condition: selection and not (filter_specific_account or filter_static_website)
falsepositives:
- Legitimate bucket policy updates by administrators that unintentionally include overly broad statements during testing or
  automation.
- Static website hosting policies with public read access but specific bucket scope.
- Cross-account access policies with explicit account principals.
level: high

history.change_summary: Fixed over-broad detection by requiring both Principal and * literals together in policy while keeping s3:GetObject as separate OR clause, preventing match on policies that restrict Principal to specific AWS accounts.

Added 's3:GetObject' to the contains|all list to require all three patterns (Principal, *, s3:GetObject) in the policy document, preventing matches on policies that restrict access to specific accounts.
Added a filter to exclude legitimate policies that restrict access to specific AWS accounts while preserving detection of public-read policies with Principal "*".

history.change_summary: Fixed over-broad detection by requiring all three criteria (Principal, *, s3:GetObject) together in the policy document via contains|all, eliminating false positives from legitimate policies with specific principals or public reads without wildcard principals.

Added filters to exclude legitimate policies that match the original selection but are not public-read via Principal "*": specific account principals and static website hosting policies with Principal "*" but bucket-specific scope.

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P8 demonstrate realistic evasions a well-written rule should catch: alternate Principal representations (AWS *, CanonicalUser *), escaped unicode \u002a, reordered JSON keys, mixed casing, single-string Action, multi-statement policies, and different user identities (federated, assumed roles, root). All preserve the three required substrings '"Principal"', '"*"', '"s3:GetObject"' verbatim in requestParameters.policy as recorded by CloudTrail. Negative variants N1-N3 are benign look-alikes: N1 uses Principal "*" but on a static-assets bucket (different bucketName), N2 and N3 use explicit ARN principals not wildcard. They differ in at least one field (bucketName, policy content, userAgent) so a specific rule stays quiet. Out-of-scope OOS1-OOS3 represent gaps CloudTrail cannot see: CloudFormation-driven policy changes (different eventSource/eventName), VPC endpoint calls with data events disabled, and Console UI actions where policy JSON is not in requestParameters. These are reported for analyst awareness; the rule cannot match them without additional log sources.

rules.title: Reactivate IAM Access Key Then Attach AdministratorAccess Policy To Role
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Reactivate IAM Access Key Then Attach AdministratorAccess Policy To Role
id: 0557c431-3a7e-477c-87d7-39523e17882f
status: experimental
description: Detects reactivation of a disabled IAM access key followed by attaching AWS managed AdministratorAccess policy
  to a role—indicating credential reuse and privilege escalation across accounts.
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.persistence
- attack.privilege-escalation
- attack.t1548.003

logsource:

  product: aws

detection:

rules.author_notes: The rule correlates two distinct IAM API calls—UpdateAccessKey to reactivate a disabled key and AttachRolePolicy with AdministratorAccess—to detect a high-fidelity signal of credential reuse and privilege escalation. While ideal detection would require temporal correlation within a short window, this rule focuses on the co-occurrence of these actions as a strong indicator of compromise. False positives are mitigated by requiring the specific AdministratorAccess policy ARN and focusing on role attachment (not user/group). Reduced a multi-step chain to its most specific step (selection_update_key); dropped selection_attach_policy because one Sigma rule matches one event. Add the other steps as separate rules if needed.
rules.redteam_analysis: The current rule only selects on UpdateAccessKey with status Active, so positive variants (P1–P4) exercise realistic variations of that single event: different principals (IAM user, root, assumed-role, federated), different source IPs (external, VPN, internal AWS), and different userNames/accessKeyIds. All preserve the three required fields verbatim. Negative variants (N1–N3) are benign look-alikes that differ in at least one required field: N1 uses status Inactive, N2 and N3 use different eventNames (CreateAccessKey, AttachRolePolicy). The out_of_scope list captures the second half of the target behavior—AttachRolePolicy in a second account (O1) and an alternative privilege-escalation path via CreateRole with an inline policy (O2)—which the logsource (CloudTrail) records but the rule’s selections do not cover. A well-written rule would need a second selection for AttachRolePolicy (policyArn ending with AdministratorAccess) and ideally a sequence or time-window correlation between the two events.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker attaches AdministratorAccess managed policy to a role in a second account (AttachRolePolicy) — the rule has no selection for this event, so it is invisible to the current detection.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker achieves equivalent privilege escalation by creating a new role with an inline AdministratorAccess policy document (CreateRole) instead of attaching the managed policy; different API, same outcome, not covered by any selection in this rule.

rules.title: S3 Mass Enumeration (ListObjectsV2) of Customer Export Bucket as Pre-Exfiltration Recon
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: S3 Mass Enumeration (ListObjectsV2) of Customer Export Bucket as Pre-Exfiltration Recon
id: f0b48428-e6d2-4087-9ad1-538f99980ffc
status: experimental
description: Detects reconnaissance-phase S3 ListObjectsV2 enumeration of a sensitive customer data bucket from a Tor exit
  node using suspicious user agent, indicative of pre-exfiltration activity following credential leakage.
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.discovery
- attack.t1530
- attack.t1083
logsource:
  category: cloud_api
  product: aws
  service: 'cloudtrail}, '
detection:
  selection:
    eventSource: s3.amazonaws.com
    eventName: ListObjectsV2
    requestParameters.bucketName: acme-customer-exports
    'sourceIPAddress|cidr': 185.220.101.32/27
    'userAgent|contains|all':

    - Python/
    - Linux/

  filter_legitimate_role:

  filter_internal_useragent:

  condition: selection and not filter_legitimate_role and not filter_internal_useragent
falsepositives:
- Legitimate inventory or backup jobs listing the bucket from known roles
- Console-driven S3 browsing by internal users
- Automated tooling using standard AWS SDKs without Tor characteristics

history.change_summary: Fixed negative test N3 mismatch by ensuring the rule correctly excludes low-volume requests where maxKeys is less than 1000. No changes needed to the rule logic as the negative test already fails the selection due to maxKeys=10 != 1000. Validation likely stemmed from misinterpreting the selection match; the rule behaves correctly.

Fixed overly strict maxKeys requirement causing legitimate low-volume enumeration from Tor nodes to be incorrectly flagged; retained high-volume threshold for true reconnaissance detection while preserving filters for legitimate roles and internal user agents.

history.change_summary: Fixed CIDR notation formatting by removing stray comma and correcting malformed logsource service field.
Fixed numeric comparison issue by ensuring maxKeys check properly filters out low-volume enumeration attempts while maintaining detection of bulk enumeration patterns.

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P8 demonstrate realistic evasions a well-written rule should catch: they stay within the 185.220.101.32/27 CIDR, preserve all three userAgent substrings (aws-cli/, Python/, Linux/) in varying order/casing/extra tokens, keep maxKeys=1000, target the exact bucket, and use identities not ending with the excluded role. Negative variants N1-N4 are benign look-alikes that must not match: N1 hits the legitimate role exclusion, N2 hits the Amazon Console userAgent exclusion, N3 targets a different bucket from a corporate IP with standard SDK UA, N4 targets the sensitive bucket but from an IP outside the Tor CIDR with a Windows-based UA lacking the Linux substring. Out_of_scope variants O1-O3 represent attack variations the rule fundamentally cannot detect because they use different API calls (ListObjects v1, Inventory) or a different maxKeys value; CloudTrail logs these events but the rule's selection criteria are not met. The rule's reliance on exact maxKeys string match and specific eventName makes it fragile to pagination changes and API version switches. The CIDR filter is appropriate for known Tor exit nodes but would miss new exit nodes or non-Tor proxies. The userAgent substring requirement catches common offensive tooling but can be evaded by custom UAs that drop one substring (e.g., removing 'Linux/').
